Could a planet really
orbit a supermassive black
hole, close enough to
slow its time by
tens of thousands of
times, and survive?
Physics says only under
extreme conditions.
What kind of black
hole would it take?
A planet simply cannot
survive at the precipice
of an ordinary,
non-rotating Schwarzschild
black hole.
In a non-rotating system,
the region needed for
a time-dilation factor
of tens of thousands
to one lies so
close to the event
horizon that circular orbits
become completely unstable.
The theoretical breakthrough
came in 1963,
when the New Zealand
mathematician Roy Kerr
solved Einstein's field
equations for a spinning mass.
A spinning Kerr black
hole drags the structure
of space and time
around with it,
like honey stirred by
a high-speed blender.
This dragging of reality
is known as frame-dragging,
or the Lense-Thirring effect.
Close to a Kerr
black hole, space itself
is swept around at
nearly the speed of light.
The minimum distance at
which a planet can
safely orbit without
plunging inward moves
dramatically closer to
the event horizon.
However, spin alone is
not enough.
The black hole must
also be unfathomably large.
If you placed a
planet next to a
stellar black hole ten
times the mass of
the Sun, the pull
on the near side
of the planet would
be far stronger than
the pull on the far side.
These differences, called
tidal forces, would stretch
the planet like taffy
and tear it to pieces.
But if the black
hole has the mass
of one hundred million
Suns, the tidal stretch
across a planet becomes
remarkably gentle.
The theoretical physicist
Kip Thorne, a Nobel
laureate, calculated what
kind of spin would
be required for the
three-hour to
twenty-three-year ratio
on a surviving world.
The supermassive black
hole must spin at
about 99.999999999999
percent of its theoretical
maximum rate.
He showed that while
the conditions required
are extraordinarily rare,
demanding a precise
combination of mass,
spin, and orbital radius,
not a single law
of physics is broken.
The universe does not
forbid a world where
three hours equal
twenty-three years.
It demands an extreme
laboratory of gravity that
pushes reality to its limits.
The full story,
with the giant waves
and the one-way ticket
through time, is on
Miya's Lab.
